{{Short description|French demographer and statistician}}
'''Lucien March''' (6 December 1859 – 4 April 1933) was a French demographer, statistician, and engineer.<ref name="Armatte">{{cite journal |last1=Armatte |first1=Michel |year=2005 |title=Lucien March (1859-1933): une statistique mathématique sans probabilité? |url=https://eudml.org/doc/124587 |journal=Journal Électronique d'Histoire des Probabilités et de la Statistique [electronic only] |volume=1 |issue=1}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author=Desrosières |first=Alain |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hqO0Qvjy4HsC |title=The Politics of Large Numbers: A History of Statistical Reasoning |publisher=Harvard University Press |year=2002 |isbn=9780674009691 |location=Cambridge |postscript=; trans. by Camille Naish from {{lang|fr|La politique des grand nombres: Histoire de la raison statistique}} (1993)}}</ref><ref name=Obit>{{cite journal|author=Huber, Michel|title=Nécrologie: Lucien March (1859–1933)|journal=Revue d'économie politique|date=1933 |volume=47|issue=2|pages=545–547|jstor=24685765}}</ref>

In 1878 Lucien March enrolled in l'[[École polytechnique]] and after graduation in 1880<ref name=Obit/> served in the naval artillery corps.<ref name=Armatte/> He was the director of the {{Ill|Statistique générale de la France|fr}} (SGF) from 1896 to 1920. In 1896, he introduced [[Hollerith]] [[punched card]] [[tabulating machine]]s into France and later invented an improved machine, the classifier-counter-printer, which was used until the 1940s. He also arranged a sorting process using the workplace addresses of the people counted in the French population census to generate valuable economic data and labor statistics.<ref>{{cite book|title=The Politics of Large Numbers|year=2002|page=158}}</ref>

He was an invited speaker of the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] (ICM) in Rome (1908), Toronto (1924), and Bologna (1928).<ref>March, L. "Note sur la corrélation." In ''Atti del Congresso Internazionale dei Matematici: Bologna del 3 al 10 de settembre di 1928'', vol. 6, pp. 133–148. 1929.</ref>

In 1912, upon his return from an international congress on eugenics, held in London, March helped to found a French eugenics society, which published in 1922 {{Lang|fr|Eugénique et Sélection}}, a collection of essays on [[eugenics]].<ref>{{cite book|title=The Politics of Large Numbers|year=2002|page=161}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Papenoe |first=Paul |date=1 September 1923 |title=Eugenics in France |journal=[[Journal of Heredity]] |volume=14 |issue=6 |pages=275–276 |doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.jhered.a102339}}</ref> In the 1920s he played an important role in the [[International Federation of Eugenics Organizations]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hodson |first=C. B. S. |date=1934 |title=Lucien March: An appreciation |journal=[[The Eugenics Review]] |volume=25 |issue=4 |pages=261 |pmid=21260113 |pmc=2985286}}</ref>
